Since it uses some nebulous terminology that a new user may not understand, let's try to translate /u/rocket_robin_hood's post in an ELI5 way for you:

Forking is creating a different project path for one reason or another. So, let's pretend that a coding project to create a Minesweeper game is being made, but you think it should look more like the classic Windows Minesweeper, but I think it should look more modern. We can take the existing code for the project and fork it into two separate projects for the two of us. Both of these come from the same source, but end up on two separate and parallel paths. Drawing these paths out looks like a fork, and thus, it's called forking.

On the display manager point, you have a display manager which allows your screen to render your mouse, desktop, office software, etc. This display manager is old... like, really really old... X11 is so old that a new display manager is currently being created, called Wayland. Well, Canonical (the company behind Ubuntu) felt that wasn't good enough, and they wanted control over the new window manager that would be running on every machine in existence. So, instead of helping develop Wayland, they forked the project and created Mir. Mir is trying to accomplish everything Wayland is, but Canonical wants to control the project and what is done with it.

Gnome3 is the desktop environment (taskbar, start menu, desktop icons, right-click menu, etc) rendered by your display manager, which you use for many Linux distributions. Ubuntu was using it, but like Mir, Canonical wanted to control the user interface, so they forked the Gnome project and created the Unity desktop environment. This DE is a GIANT resource hog, is slow and difficult to use, and ultimately the reason most people left Ubuntu for Mint or other distros. It's also the way Canonical was able to implement Amazon tracking into your desktop, which is a point of contention you seem to already be familiar with.

Daemons are the Linux equivalent of Windows services. They run in the background and perform menial tasks for the user (such as running a printer when you want to print a document, or automatically connecting amongst your ethernet card and all of you known wireless networks when connected or in range), so that the system works correctly... which is where systemd comes from: system daemon. And, while systemd isn't perfect, it became a big player in the Linux world, and Debian itself (Ubuntu is based/built off of the Debian distro). But Canonical (once again) wasn't happy about not having control over the user experience... so they created their own daemon/service controller.

Essentially, it all boils down to Canonical not wanting to play nice with the Linux community and wanting to control everything about the user experience... which isn't very Linux-ish. Linux is supposed to be extremely open and user-friendly, but Canonical has locked many features out of Ubuntu. For instance, it's such a pain in the ass to run a custom kernel with Ubuntu... so much so that you're better off just learning a new distro altogether.

Well, to more concisely answer your OP, that is exactly "what happened to Ubuntu." Canonical started making changes which weren't Linux-ish, and people were afraid of this very thing. So many started leaving. If you look up Canonical, you'll find their information mixed in with a lot of hate. I don't think I've ever seen a user supporting Canonical or what they do.

You have the issue of selling adspace on your desktop... which should be enough of a reason to leave and never go back. Even if you're able to turn it off, the fact that the modules exist for Canonical to view your habits and "suggest" Amazon products for you should be enough to send people running... which is why many people are leaving Win10... this exact reason.

Then you have the money issue and the Kubuntu/UCC debacle that happened a few months ago, which is why I left the _buntu family altogether:

Back in the day, Ubuntu was the king of "newbie distros" for people first getting into Linux. It got so big, so fast, that it ended up forking itself many different times over. As stated above, it used to be Gnome2 before they changed to Gnome3, which they later forked into Unity... but some users didn't want Gnome3 or Unity, so some used XFCE, or KDE, or LXDE, or stuck with Gnome2, or something crazy.

I know that was a lot of acronyms, but it all boils down to different desktop environments. Think about Windows 95 vs XP vs Vista vs Win8... they're all Windows at their core, but they look and behave VERY differently. These different desktop environments were all Ubuntu at their core, but their desktops and "Start menus" looked and behaved very differently, and they used a different window manager (Windows Explorer), and they came with different programs (to view pictures, edit text documents, etc.).

Because all of these users wanted different things, forks of Ubuntu became a trend and Kubuntu (KDE Ubuntu), Xubuntu (XFCE Ubuntu), Lubuntu (LXDE Ubuntu), Ubuntu Mate (Gnome2 Ubuntu), and other distros were born. But, again, Canonical wanted control over all of these things, so they created the Ubuntu Community Council (UCC). Canonical unsurprisingly announced that they will be heading this council, and (indirectly) the distros attached.

The purpose of the UCC was to organize each of these distros so that they were working together instead of against each other (which is weird for Canonical -- see Wayland vs Mir). It also helped organize the funding for each distro that came from donations as well as the Ubuntu app store.

But Johnathan Riddell (the head of Kubuntu) wasn't happy with this. Since Canonical was in charge of the UCC (as well as the funding), Riddell wanted transparency for the funding. He pushed the issue until 2009/2010 when Canonical declared that Kubuntu was no longer going to be a recognized Ubuntu derivation, and would no longer be part of the UCC... and therefore no longer receive funding "from" Canonical.

So Riddell created the Kubuntu Council (KC) and the Kubuntu users/community actually elected (he didn't appoint himself) him as its "head." Kubuntu goes their own route, and they become HUGE. Given the Unity failure and the poor publicity Canonical was getting, many Ubuntu users fled and flocked to Kubuntu. Whereas Ubuntu was locking out Linux features (see using a custom kernel), KDE/Kubuntu was all about customization and being at the "forefront" of user features.

Fast forward to a few months ago, and the UCC sent a letter to the KC stating that, due to Riddell's "behavior," he was to "step down" from his elected position, and Kubuntu was to be re-absorbed into the UCC under Canonical's control. This was obviously ignored by the KC and Riddell, as it should have been, and this "bad publicity" sent EVEN MORE users running from Ubuntu in droves.
